content:
Dozens of pages of presidential briefings were declassified on Friday, the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, detailing the intelligence gathered by government officials about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda before the hijackings that killed nearly 3,000 people and forever changed the face of US national security.

The documents show how security analysts tracked bin Laden's movements and support networks, as well as concerns about possible threats to American targets. They also detail officials' understanding of his networks in the US and other countries, including how his operations were funded.

CIA Director John Ratcliffe called the move an "act of tremendous transparency" and said it was the largest single release of Presidential Daily Briefings by the CIA — highly classified briefings prepared by the intelligence community for the nation's top leaders.

The documents span a wide range, from a February 1998 briefing prepared for then-President Clinton titled "Terrorist Groups Seeking Sophisticated WMD Capabilities" that mentioned bin Laden and other Islamic extremists, to a September 12, 2001 report in which sources said the attack plot had been in the works for two years and had also targeted the US Capitol.

An April 1998 document described the Taliban's reluctance to hand over bin Laden, who was considered a "guest" of the Taliban in Afghanistan, noting the group was "grateful for his assistance during the Soviet occupation" and therefore "unwilling to offend him by surveilling or restricting his activities."

A July 1998 briefer said it was reasonable to assume "bin Laden will select a target for attack in the US" and noted he was "interested in conducting chemical and biological attacks."

Two months later, a briefer wrote that bin Laden's "first preference" was to "conduct attacks in the United States, in Washington," and that al-Qaeda "could fly an explosives-laden aircraft into a US city."

Possible hijackings were also discussed in December 1998, when a briefer described planners who "had recently evaded security during a recent trial at an unspecified New York airport" and said "parts of the bin Laden network have received hijacking training."

Other documents detail bin Laden's search for materials for a "dirty bomb" — a conventional weapon infused with radioactive material. Intelligence officials said that by June 1999, his operatives had been experimenting with such devices to "enhance the explosive energy output."

About two years before the attack, intelligence officials knew bin Laden appeared to be concealing from the Taliban his intention to launch an unprovoked strike against the US. Briefings prepared for President George W. Bush in early 2001 focused in part on bin Laden's "rudimentary effort to experiment with producing and deploying a biological weapon."

A report a month before the attack noted bin Laden was "determined to strike the US with a terrorist attack" and said al-Qaeda's 1998 bombings of US embassies "demonstrated that he will spend years preparing an operation and will not be deterred by setbacks."

In the same period — August 2001 — officials noted in a report "suspicious activity inside this country consistent with preparations for hijackings or other types of attacks, including recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York," and added that the FBI "was conducting approximately 70 full field investigations throughout the country that it considered bin Laden-related."

Many of the documents are redacted to hide the names of sources and other identifying information. The documents do not appear to yield major breakthroughs in the understanding of the attack-planning process or how US officials came to understand what happened.

In the years after the attack, a bipartisan commission pointed to a lack of intelligence sharing between agencies like the CIA and FBI and made a series of recommendations that led to the creation of new positions, including the director of national intelligence, and the National Counterterrorism Center, which analyzes terrorism information at home and abroad.

Asked about the declassification, the White House noted that the National Archives also declassified another set of documents on Friday. Those include interviews with national security officials from the Clinton and Bush administrations, the product of a commission that investigated the attacks from 2002 to 2004.
